claims.text: Algorithmic bias reduces consumers' acceptance intention of AI recommendations.
The negative effect of algorithmic bias on acceptance intention is more pronounced under similarity-based recommendation strategies compared to relevance-based recommendation strategies.
Relevance-based recommendations enhance recommendation acceptance intention relative to similarity-based recommendations by reducing self-identity threat.
Perceived warmth moderates the mediation pathway of self-identity threat between recommendation strategy and acceptance intention.
Privacy concerns moderate the mediation pathway of self-identity threat between recommendation strategy and acceptance intention.
Similarity-based recommendations may exacerbate user resistance in the context of algorithmic bias.

evidence.description: Through four experimental studies (total N = 895), the authors find that algorithmic bias reduces consumers' acceptance intention.

Four experimental studies (total N = 895) show that the reduction in acceptance intention from algorithmic bias is more pronounced under similarity-based (vs. relevance-based) recommendation strategies.
Results indicate that relevance-based recommendations (vs. similarity-based recommendations) enhance recommendation acceptance intention by reducing self-identity threat.
Findings demonstrate that perceived warmth moderates the mediation pathway of self-identity threat.
Findings demonstrate that privacy concerns moderate the mediation pathway of self-identity threat.
Empirical results from four experimental studies reveal that similarity-based recommendations may exacerbate user resistance in the context of algorithmic bias.

methodologies.name: Experimental consumer behavioral studies
methodologies.description: Four experimental studies examining the impact of algorithmic bias and recommendation strategies (relevance-based vs. similarity-based) on consumer acceptance intention, mediated by self-identity threat and moderated by perceived warmth and privacy concerns.

limitations.text: How different recommendation strategies interact with algorithmic bias to influence consumers' psychological responses in intelligent recommendation scenarios remains underexplored.
